Right: the complete bipartite graph K3,3, nodes A, B, C each joined to D, E, F, drawn with a single crossing, marked in the accent color. Its 9 edges are within the 3n - 6 bound of 12, but no drawing avoids every crossing, so is_planar() returns False." width="100%"} A graph is planar if it can be drawn in the plane without any two edges crossing. This is an exact test: it runs the left-right planarity test (Brandes' formulation of de Fraysseix and Rosenstiehl's criterion) in linear time, like NetworkX's `is_planar()`. Edge direction, self-loops and parallel edges make no difference to planarity, so they are ignored. Use `check_planarity()` to get a crossing-free arrangement of the edges around each node when the graph is planar, or the Kuratowski subgraph that rules it out when it is not, and `layout_planar()` to draw a planar graph without crossings. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the graph is planar, `False` otherwise. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~check_planarity`) : The test with its certificate: an embedding or a Kuratowski subgraph. [](`~layout_planar`) : Positions that draw a planar graph without edge crossings. ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Euler's formula $n - e + f = 2$ for a connected planar drawing, together with every face of a simple planar graph being bounded by at least three edges, gives the edge bound $e \le 3n - 6$ for $n \ge 3$. A graph above the bound is rejected at once; otherwise a depth-first search orients the edges and the test checks whether its back edges can be split into a left and a right side without conflicts. By Kuratowski's theorem a graph is planar exactly when it contains no subdivision of $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$, so graphs that pass the edge bound can still be non-planar: $K_{3,3}$ has 9 edges against a bound of 12, and the Petersen graph 15 against 24. ## Examples {.doc-examples} `K_4` is planar: draw one node inside the triangle of the other three. ::: {#a349be1f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec ec.Graph().add_full_graph(n=4).is_planar() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: `K_5` is not; its 10 edges are already more than `3 * 5 - 6 = 9`: ::: {#759bf4ab .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph().add_full_graph(n=5).is_planar() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: ::: `K_{3,3}` is not planar either, although it is well inside the edge bound: ::: {#762fb299 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph().add_complete_bipartite_graph(3, 3).is_planar() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` False ``` ::: ::: The Petersen graph contains a subdivision of `K_{3,3}`, so it is not planar: ::: {#30f9f478 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph().add_named_graph("petersen").is_planar() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Trees and grids are planar at any size: ::: {#85887856 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} grid = ec.Graph().add_grid_2d(rows=20, cols=20) grid.is_planar() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` True ``` ::: :::
